track.name: excel
track.label: Excel for Business
track.summary: Everyday Excel for running a business, from the first formula to automated reporting: lookups, tables, pivots, charts, what-if planning and the tools that remove manual work.

phases.title: Excel Fundamentals
phases.description: The interface, formulas, cell references, and the handful of functions that cover most day-to-day work.

phases.title: Lookups & Data Cleaning
phases.description: Pull data across sheets reliably and keep it clean with validation rules.

phases.title: Visualization & Dashboards
phases.description: Charts, conditional formatting, and a dashboard someone else could actually read.

phases.title: Automation & Power Tools
phases.description: Power Query, Power Pivot, and enough VBA to stop doing the same thing by hand every week.

phases.title: PivotTables & PivotCharts for Business Reporting
phases.description: Turn a raw export into a report a manager can actually read: build, filter and chart a PivotTable from scratch.

phases.title: What-If Analysis: Pricing, Staffing & Budgets
phases.description: Goal Seek, Scenario Manager and Data Tables — the three built-in tools for testing an assumption before it's a decision.

phases.title: Modern Formulas: Dynamic Arrays, LET & LAMBDA
phases.description: The formula engine current Excel actually runs on: functions that spill across a range, names for intermediate steps, and your own custom functions.

phases.title: Core Business Trackers: Budgets, Sales & Inventory
phases.description: Apply everything so far to three workbooks every business needs: a budget, a sales pipeline, and an inventory tracker.

phases.title: Workforce & Project Trackers
phases.description: Three more workbooks that come up in almost every business: a headcount plan, a project/time tracker, and an invoice template.

phases.title: Collaboration & Workbook Safety
phases.description: Work on the same workbook as other people without stepping on each other, and know how to lock down and recover a workbook.

phases.title: Next-Gen Automation: Office Scripts, Power Automate & Copilot
phases.description: Automation beyond VBA: cloud-native scripts, workflows triggered outside the workbook, and an AI assistant built into Excel.

phases.title: Building Robust, Maintainable Workbooks
phases.description: The capstone habits: trace and catch formula errors, structure a workbook so the next person can follow it, and keep a large one fast.

topics.title: The Excel Interface & Navigation
topics.description: The ribbon, cells, sheets, and the keyboard habits that make everything else faster.

steps.d: Open each ribbon tab (Home, Insert, Data, Formulas) once and note the three or four commands you'll use most.
Use Ctrl+Arrow keys to jump to the edge of a data range, and Ctrl+Home to return to A1.
Select a whole column with Ctrl+Space and a whole row with Shift+Space instead of dragging.
Add a new sheet, rename its tab, and move between sheets with Ctrl+PageUp/PageDown.

steps.t: Freeze panes on a long sheet
steps.d: Freeze the header row on a large dataset so it stays visible while you scroll.

topics.title: Formulas & Cell References
topics.description: Relative vs. absolute references, and why a dragged formula breaks without them.

steps.d: Enter =A2*B2 and drag it down a column, watching the row numbers update automatically.
Rewrite a formula with $B$1 so dragging it keeps pointing at one fixed tax-rate or fee cell.
Build a formula that locks the column but not the row (or vice versa) and drag it both across and down.
Write a formula that pulls a value from a different sheet, e.g. =Summary!B2.
Take a formula that returns the wrong value after being copied, and find which reference should have been absolute.

topics.title: Core Functions: SUM, AVERAGE, IF, COUNT
topics.description: The handful of functions that cover most day-to-day spreadsheet work.

steps.d: Use =SUM(range) instead of adding cells one by one, and confirm it updates when a value changes.
Use =AVERAGE(range) on the same data and compare it to the total.
Write =IF(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false) to label rows as "Over budget" or "On budget".
Use =COUNTIF(range, criteria) to count how many rows meet one condition.
Nest one function inside another, e.g. =IF(SUM(range)>1000, "High", "Low").

topics.title: Excel Tables & Structured References
topics.description: Turn a plain range into a real Excel Table so formatting, formulas and filters survive as data grows, and reference columns by name instead of cell address.

steps.t: Convert a range to a Table
steps.d: Select your data and press Ctrl+T (or Home > Format as Table), confirming the header row.
Use Table Design > Table Name to give it a short, meaningful name instead of the default "Table1".
Reference a column by name, e.g. =SUM(Sales[Amount]), instead of a cell range.
Turn on Table Design > Total Row and pick SUM, AVERAGE or COUNT from the dropdown for a column.
Type a new row directly below the table and check that formulas and formatting extend to it without manual work.

topics.title: Logical, Text & Date Functions
topics.description: The functions behind most real business logic: nested conditions, splitting and joining text, and date math for deadlines and durations.

steps.d: Write a formula that only returns "Approved" when two conditions are both true, using =IF(AND(...), ...).
Use LEFT, RIGHT or MID with FIND to pull a first and last name out of one "Full Name" column.
Use TEXTJOIN with a delimiter to combine city, state and zip into one address field, skipping any blanks.
Use EDATE to add a fixed number of months to an invoice date, or WORKDAY to add working days.
Use NETWORKDAYS to find how many working days are left until a project deadline, excluding weekends.

topics.title: VLOOKUP Fundamentals
topics.description: Pull a value from another table by matching an id — the most-used lookup in business Excel.

steps.d: Use =VLOOKUP(id, table, column_number, FALSE) to pull a name or price from a lookup table by id.
Set the fourth argument to FALSE and confirm the formula returns #N/A instead of a wrong approximate match.
Add $ signs to the table_array argument so the formula still points at the right table after you copy it down.
Point table_array at a range on a different sheet instead of the same one.
Wrap the VLOOKUP in IFERROR so a missing id shows "Not found" instead of #N/A.

topics.title: INDEX & MATCH
topics.description: The more flexible lookup combo that doesn't break when columns get inserted.

steps.d: Use =MATCH(value, range, 0) to find which row a value sits in.
Use =INDEX(range, row_number) to return the value at a given position.
Nest MATCH inside INDEX so one formula finds the row and returns the value in one step.
Insert a new column into the source table and confirm the INDEX/MATCH formula still works while a VLOOKUP would break.
Return a value from a column to the left of the lookup column, which VLOOKUP can't do.

topics.title: Data Validation & Dropdown Lists
topics.description: Restrict what can be typed into a cell so a shared sheet stays clean.

steps.d: Use Data > Data Validation > List to build a dropdown from a set of allowed values.

steps.t: Source the list from a range
steps.d: Point the validation list at a named range or Table column instead of typing values directly into the dialog.
Add a short input message that explains what's expected before someone types anything.
Set a Stop-style error alert with a clear message for when someone pastes in an invalid value.
Try entering an invalid value yourself to confirm the validation actually blocks it.

topics.title: XLOOKUP, INDEX/MATCH/XMATCH — The Modern Lookup Toolkit
topics.description: XLOOKUP replaces VLOOKUP in current Excel: it searches in any direction, defaults to an exact match, and pairs with XMATCH for more flexible position-finding.

steps.d: Rewrite an existing VLOOKUP formula as =XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array) and compare the results.
Add the if_not_found argument, e.g. =XLOOKUP(id, ids, names, "Not found"), instead of wrapping the formula in IFERROR.
Return a value from a column to the left of the lookup column — something plain VLOOKUP cannot do.
Use =XMATCH(value, range) to get a row or column number, then feed it into INDEX.
Note when you'd still reach for INDEX/MATCH — for example a workbook that must stay compatible with Excel 2019 or earlier.

topics.title: Sorting, Filtering & Cleaning Data at Scale
topics.description: Go beyond a single click on the filter arrow: multi-level sorts, criteria-based filtering, and the fastest ways to clean up messy pasted data.

steps.t: Sort by more than one column
steps.d: Use Data > Sort to sort a list by Department, then by Name within each department.
Create a custom list (e.g. Small, Medium, Large) so a sort follows that order instead of alphabetical.
Set up a criteria range and use Data > Advanced to filter for rows matching several conditions at once.
Use Data > Remove Duplicates on a pasted list, choosing which columns must match to count as a duplicate.

steps.t: Split or combine text with Flash Fill
steps.d: Type one example of the pattern you want (e.g. a full name split into first/last) and press Ctrl+E to fill the rest.

topics.title: Charts That Communicate
topics.description: Picking and building the right chart for the point you're making.

steps.d: Select a data range and use Insert > Recommended Charts to see Excel's best-fit suggestions.

steps.t: Compare a bar and a line chart
steps.d: Chart the same data both ways and decide which better supports the point you're making — comparison vs. trend.
Remove gridlines and a legend the chart doesn't need, and add a clear title stating the takeaway.
Change the color of a single bar or point to draw the eye to the number that matters most.
Move and resize the chart so it sits cleanly next to the data it's built from.

topics.title: Conditional Formatting
topics.description: Formatting rules driven by formulas, not just Excel's built-in presets.

steps.d: Use Home > Conditional Formatting > Color Scales on a column of numbers to see a preset rule in action.
Use a "Greater Than" rule to flag any cell over a threshold, like a budget limit.
Use New Rule > Use a formula to highlight a whole row based on one cell's value, e.g. overdue status.
Apply data bars to a column so relative size is visible at a glance without reading every number.
Use Manage Rules to check and reorder rules when more than one could apply to the same cell.

topics.title: Building an Interactive Dashboard
topics.description: Combine pivots, slicers, and charts into one page someone else can actually use.

steps.d: Reserve one sheet for the dashboard, separate from the raw data and any working formulas.
Build a PivotTable elsewhere, then place its PivotChart on the dashboard sheet.
Insert a slicer and position it so it clearly filters the chart next to it.
Hide row/column headers and gridlines on the dashboard sheet so it reads like a report, not a spreadsheet.

steps.t: Test it as a viewer would
steps.d: Click through every slicer button yourself to confirm the whole dashboard updates correctly.

topics.title: Sparklines, Waterfall & Combo Charts
topics.description: The advanced chart types business reporting actually calls for: a trend in one cell, a bridge from budget to actual, and two series on two scales.

steps.t: Add sparklines to a summary table
steps.d: Insert a Line sparkline next to each product's monthly totals so the trend is visible without a full chart.

steps.t: Highlight the high and low points
steps.d: Turn on the High Point and Low Point markers on a sparkline to flag the best and worst month at a glance.
Chart a bridge from starting budget to ending budget, with each expense or gain as its own floating bar.
Plot actual revenue as columns and target revenue as a line on the same chart, using a secondary axis if the scales differ.

steps.t: Pick the right chart for the claim
steps.d: For one existing report, decide whether a bar, line or combo chart best supports the point it's making, and rebuild it if not.

topics.title: Power Query Basics
topics.description: Import and clean data from multiple sources without manual copy-paste.

steps.t: Import a CSV with Power Query
steps.d: Use Data > Get Data > From Text/CSV instead of copy-pasting a CSV export into a sheet.
In the Power Query Editor, delete unneeded columns and rename the rest to clear labels.
Fix a column Power Query imported as text but should be a number or date.
Close & Load the query into a Table in the workbook, instead of leaving it as a connection only.
Update the source file and click Refresh to confirm the query picks up the new data automatically.

topics.title: Power Pivot & the Data Model
topics.description: Combine multiple tables into one model you can pivot across.

topics.title: Intro to Macros & VBA
topics.description: Record a macro, then read just enough VBA to tweak it.

steps.d: Use Developer > Record Macro, perform a repetitive formatting task, then stop recording.
Run the recorded macro on a fresh copy of the same data and confirm it repeats the steps exactly.
Open the VBA editor (Alt+F11) and read through the code the recorder produced, line by line.
Add a button on the sheet and assign the macro to it so it can be run with one click.
Save the file as .xlsm so the macro is preserved next time it's opened.

topics.title: Power Query for Recurring Reports
topics.description: Build a query once and refresh it every week instead of rebuilding the report by hand: folder imports, parameters, and refresh settings.

steps.d: Point Power Query at Data > Get Data > From Folder for a set of weekly CSV exports and combine them into one table.

steps.t: Add a parameter for the file path
steps.d: Replace a hard-coded folder path with a parameter so next month's report only needs the parameter value changed.
Turn on "Refresh data when opening the file" in Connection Properties so the report is current every time it's opened.

steps.t: Handle a source that changes shape
steps.d: Add an error-tolerant step (e.g. Remove Errors or a try/otherwise) so one bad row doesn't break the whole refresh.
Rename each applied step to a plain description of what it does, so the next person can follow the transformation.

topics.title: VBA Fundamentals Beyond the Recorder
topics.description: The macro recorder only gets you so far — variables, loops and conditionals let you write VBA that adapts instead of replaying the exact same clicks.

steps.d: Write Dim total As Double and use it to accumulate a running total inside a procedure.
Use For Each cell In Range("A1:A100") to check or change every cell in a range one at a time.
Write an If/ElseIf/Else block that applies a different formatting rule depending on a cell's value.

steps.t: Combine a loop with a condition
steps.d: Loop through a column and use If inside the loop to flag or skip rows that don't meet a criterion.
Take a macro the recorder produced and remove the parts that only worked because of the exact selection you made — replace them with a loop.

topics.title: Building a PivotTable for a Business Report
topics.description: Turn a raw transaction export into a summary a manager can read in ten seconds, without writing a single formula.

steps.d: Select a cell in your data (ideally an Excel Table) and choose Insert > PivotTable.
Drag a category field (e.g. Region) to Rows and a numeric field (e.g. Revenue) to Values.
Switch a Values field from Sum to Average or Count and see how the report changes.
Sort the rows highest-to-lowest and rename "Sum of Revenue" to a plain label like "Revenue ($)".
Add a few new rows to the source data, then right-click the PivotTable and Refresh.

topics.title: PivotCharts & Slicers
topics.description: Make a PivotTable interactive: a chart that updates with it, and buttons anyone can click to change what's shown.

steps.d: From an existing PivotTable, choose PivotTable Analyze > PivotChart and pick a chart type.
Insert a slicer for a category field (e.g. Region or Product) and click a button to filter both the table and chart at once.
For a date field, insert a Timeline slicer and switch it between Months, Quarters and Years.

steps.t: Connect one slicer to two PivotTables
steps.d: Use Report Connections (Filter Connections) so one slicer filters two PivotTables built from the same source.

topics.title: Advanced Pivot Techniques
topics.description: The techniques that separate a quick summary from a polished report: date grouping, percent-of-total, and pulling one number out with a formula.

steps.t: Group dates by month or quarter
steps.d: Right-click a date field in the PivotTable and Group by Months and Quarters instead of listing every date.
Use Show Values As > % of Grand Total on a Values field to see each region's share instead of its raw number.
Add the same field twice and set the second copy to Show Values As > Running Total In.

steps.t: Pull one number out with GETPIVOTDATA
steps.d: Reference a single PivotTable value from another cell using =GETPIVOTDATA(...) instead of a plain cell reference.

topics.title: Goal Seek
topics.description: Work backward from a target result to the input that produces it — the fastest of the three what-if tools when you only need to solve for one number.

steps.t: Set up a formula with one free input
steps.d: Build a pricing formula where profit depends on a single price cell you can still change.
Use Data > What-If Analysis > Goal Seek to find the price that makes profit equal a specific target.

steps.t: Apply it to a break-even question
steps.d: Find the unit price (or sales volume) at which profit equals exactly zero.
Notice that Goal Seek only solves for one input — recognize when a question needs Scenario Manager or Solver instead.

topics.title: Scenario Manager
topics.description: Save several named sets of assumptions — best case, worst case, likely case — and switch between them without retyping a single number.

steps.d: Pick the two or three input cells (e.g. headcount, salary, growth rate) a scenario should vary.
Use Data > What-If Analysis > Scenario Manager > Add to name and save a "Best Case" set of values for those cells.

steps.t: Add a second and third scenario
steps.d: Repeat for "Likely Case" and "Worst Case" using the same changing cells with different values.
Use Show in Scenario Manager to swap the values in place and watch dependent formulas update.
Create a Scenario Summary report that lines up all scenarios and their results side by side.

topics.title: Data Tables (Sensitivity Tables)
topics.description: See every combination of one or two inputs at once, in a grid, instead of checking scenarios one at a time.

steps.d: List a column of possible interest rates or prices next to a formula, then use Data > What-If Analysis > Data Table with one input cell.
Add a row of a second variable (e.g. loan term) so the table shows every combination of two inputs at once.
Scan the table to find the combination of inputs that first crosses a target threshold, such as a minimum acceptable margin.
Switch calculation to "Automatic Except for Data Tables" if a large table is slowing the workbook down.

topics.title: Dynamic Array Functions: FILTER, SORT, UNIQUE, SEQUENCE
topics.description: Functions that return a whole range of results from one formula, spilling into the empty cells around it instead of needing to be copied down.

steps.d: Write =FILTER(range, condition) to pull every row matching a condition into a spilled list, with no helper column.
Use =UNIQUE(range) to list each distinct customer or product exactly once.
Nest UNIQUE(FILTER(...)) to get the distinct values that meet a condition in one formula.
Wrap a FILTER or UNIQUE formula in SORT so the spilled list comes out in a specific order.
Use =SEQUENCE(12) to generate 12 sequential numbers (e.g. for a 12-month template) instead of typing or dragging them.

topics.title: LET — Naming Steps Inside a Formula
topics.description: Give an intermediate calculation a name inside the formula itself, so a long formula reads like a short paragraph and only calculates each step once.

steps.d: Find an existing formula that calculates the same thing (e.g. a lookup or a subtotal) more than once.
Rewrite the formula as =LET(name, expression, calculation) so the repeated part is calculated once and reused by name.
Add a second and third name/value pair inside the same LET, using the first name inside the second's definition.
Use Alt+Enter to put each name/value pair on its own line so the formula reads top to bottom.

topics.title: LAMBDA — Writing Custom Functions
topics.description: Turn a formula you keep rebuilding into your own named function, callable like SUM or VLOOKUP, with no VBA required.

steps.t: Write and test a LAMBDA in a cell
steps.d: Build =LAMBDA(price, cost, (price-cost)/price)(B2, C2) and confirm it returns the right margin.

steps.t: Name it in the Name Manager
steps.d: Move the working LAMBDA (without the test arguments) into a defined name, e.g. MARGIN, via Formulas > Name Manager.

steps.t: Call it like a built-in function
steps.d: Use =MARGIN(B2,C2) in any cell in the workbook now that it's named.
Give the named LAMBDA a description in Name Manager so Excel's function tooltip explains what it does.
Read one example of a LAMBDA that calls itself, and note how it avoids looping forever.

topics.title: Budgets & Expense Trackers
topics.description: A workbook that tracks planned vs. actual spend by category and flags an overspend automatically.

steps.t: Lay out categories as a Table
steps.d: List expense categories down the rows and Budget/Actual/Variance across the columns, and convert the range to a Table.
Add a Variance column with =Actual-Budget so overspend shows as a positive (or negative, pick a convention and stay consistent).
Apply conditional formatting so any category over budget turns red without you checking it by eye.
Build a small PivotTable or SUMIFS summary showing total budget vs. actual by month.
Lock the Variance and summary cells and protect the sheet so only the Actual column can be edited.

topics.title: Sales & Pipeline Trackers
topics.description: A lightweight CRM: one row per deal, a stage for each, and a chart that shows where the pipeline is thin.

steps.d: One row per opportunity, with columns for Company, Value, Stage, Owner and Expected Close Date, as an Excel Table.
Add a data validation dropdown for Stage (e.g. Lead, Qualified, Proposal, Won, Lost) so it can't be typed freehand.
Build a PivotTable that totals deal Value by Stage to see how much revenue sits at each step.
Chart the stage totals as a funnel (or a horizontal stacked bar standing in for one) to show where deals drop off.
Add a conditional formatting rule that highlights any deal with no stage change in over 30 days.

topics.title: Inventory Trackers
topics.description: Track stock on hand by item, and get a clear signal for what to reorder before it runs out.

steps.d: One row per SKU with On Hand, Reorder Level and Unit Cost columns, as an Excel Table.
Add a column that multiplies On Hand by Unit Cost to get the value tied up in each item.
Use an IF formula or conditional formatting to flag any row where On Hand is at or below Reorder Level.
Sort or use an ABC-style classification to see which small number of items make up most of the inventory value.
Build a PivotTable showing total stock value by product category.

topics.title: Headcount Planning
topics.description: Plan who's on the team, when they start, and what it costs — the workbook behind every hiring conversation.

steps.d: Build a table with Role, Department, Status (Filled/Open/Planned), Start Date and Annual Cost.
Use a PivotTable or SUMIFS to total headcount cost by department for the current org.
Add planned hires with future start dates, then use a formula to show cumulative headcount and cost by month.
Use a Scenario (from Scenario Manager) to compare cost with and without the planned hires.

topics.title: Project & Time Tracking
topics.description: A simple Gantt-style project tracker plus a timesheet, without needing a separate project management tool.

steps.t: List tasks with start and duration
steps.d: Build a table of tasks with Start Date and Duration (days), and a calculated End Date column.

steps.t: Build a Gantt bar with conditional formatting
steps.d: Use conditional formatting across a row of dates to shade the cells between each task's start and end date.
Add a % Complete column and conditionally format it so overdue, incomplete tasks stand out.
Build a separate weekly timesheet table with Task, Date and Hours, and SUMIFS it back to a per-task total.

topics.title: Invoicing Templates
topics.description: A clean, reusable invoice: line items that total themselves, tax calculated automatically, and a design that looks professional.

steps.d: Add your business details, a bill-to section, an invoice number and a date, kept separate from the line items.
Create a Table with Description, Quantity, Unit Price and an Amount column that multiplies the two.
Sum the Amount column, apply a tax rate, and add a Total row using structured references.
Save the finished workbook as a .xltx template so each new invoice starts from a clean copy.
Lock the formula cells and protect the sheet, leaving only the client details and line items editable.

topics.title: Co-authoring & Comments
topics.description: Edit the same workbook as a colleague at the same time, and discuss the data in place instead of over email.

steps.t: Save a workbook to OneDrive or SharePoint
steps.d: Move a workbook off your local drive so co-authoring becomes available.
Open the same workbook as another person and notice their colored selection and cell outlines as they type.
Right-click a cell, choose New Comment, and leave feedback on a specific number instead of a whole sheet.
Type @ plus their name inside a comment so they get an email notification and a direct link to it.
Once the comment is addressed, mark it resolved so it collapses out of the way.

topics.title: Protecting Sheets & Workbooks
topics.description: Stop a shared workbook from being edited by accident: lock formulas, lock the sheet structure, or require a password to open it at all.

steps.d: Select the cells people should still be able to edit and clear "Locked" in Format Cells, before protecting anything.
Use Review > Protect Sheet with a password so every other cell becomes read-only.
Use Review > Protect Workbook to stop sheets being added, deleted, hidden or renamed.
Set a password to open the file itself via File > Info > Protect Workbook > Encrypt with Password.
Note that sheet protection isn't real security — it just prevents accidental changes, not a determined attacker.

topics.title: Version History & Safe Sharing
topics.description: Recover from a bad edit, and check a workbook for anything you didn't mean to send before it goes out the door.

steps.d: Right-click a OneDrive or SharePoint file and choose Version History to see every saved version.
Pick a version from before a mistake was made and restore it, making it the new current version.
Use File > Info > Check for Issues > Inspect Document to find hidden sheets, comments or personal information before sharing.
Clear any hidden data the inspector flags, then save a clean copy for external sharing.

topics.title: Office Scripts — Automating Excel on the Web
topics.description: The TypeScript-based successor to VBA macros for Excel on the web: record an action once, then run or share it as a button.

steps.d: Open a workbook in Excel on the web, start the Action Recorder, and perform a repetitive cleanup task.
Stop recording, save the script under a clear name describing what it does.
Open the Code Editor and read through the TypeScript the recorder produced for your actions.

steps.t: Run it again on new data
steps.d: Open a fresh copy of the source data and run the saved script to confirm it repeats the same cleanup.
Let a colleague run your script from the same workbook without opening the Code Editor themselves.

topics.title: Power Automate — Flows Triggered by Excel
topics.description: Trigger an Office Script — or a whole workflow — from outside the workbook: a schedule, a new email, or a Microsoft Forms submission.

steps.d: On the Automate tab, choose Automate Work and browse Power Automate's prebuilt Excel templates.
Create a Scheduled cloud flow that runs an Office Script against a workbook every morning.
Create an Automated flow that adds a row to a workbook whenever a Microsoft Forms response comes in.

steps.t: Run an Office Script from a flow
steps.d: Add the Excel Online (Business) "Run script" action to a flow and pass it a parameter from an earlier step.

steps.t: Test and check the run history
steps.d: Trigger the flow manually once, then check Power Automate's run history to confirm it did what you expected.

topics.title: Copilot in Excel
topics.description: An AI assistant built into Excel that can explain a workbook, generate formulas, and surface insights you'd otherwise have to go find by hand.

steps.t: Open Copilot on a real workbook
steps.d: Select the Copilot icon and ask it to summarize what a worksheet you didn't build actually contains.
Ask Copilot to find trends or outliers in a table and generate a chart or PivotTable from the answer.
Describe a calculation in plain English and have Copilot write the formula, then check it against a manual example.
Verify one Copilot-generated formula or number against a manual calculation before trusting it in a real report.

topics.title: Formula Auditing & Error Checking
topics.description: Find out what feeds a formula, what it feeds into, and why it's returning an error, before you trust the number it shows.

steps.d: Select a formula cell and use Formulas > Trace Precedents to see arrows pointing to every cell that feeds it.
Select an input cell and use Trace Dependents to see everything downstream that would change if you edited it.
Use Formulas > Error Checking to step through every flagged error in a workbook one at a time.

steps.t: Evaluate a formula step by step
steps.d: Use Evaluate Formula on a nested formula to watch it calculate one piece at a time in order.
Diagnose what's causing a #REF! or #N/A before reaching for IFERROR to hide it.

topics.title: Workbook Design & Documentation
topics.description: Structure a workbook so someone who has never seen it — including you, in six months — can understand it in a few minutes.

steps.d: Put raw inputs on their own sheet, calculations on another, and the report or summary on a third.
Use one consistent color for every input cell and another for every formula, across the whole workbook.
Rename each sheet tab to describe its contents and color-code related tabs so navigation doesn't require guessing.
Add a first tab that explains what the workbook does, where the inputs come from, and who owns it.
Add a visible check (e.g. a balance that should equal zero) that flags red the moment something stops reconciling.

topics.title: Performance & Common Pitfalls
topics.description: Keep a large workbook fast, and avoid the handful of habits that quietly make every workbook slower and more fragile than it needs to be.

steps.d: Search a workbook for formulas referencing an entire column (e.g. A:A) and narrow them to the actual data range.
Find uses of OFFSET, INDIRECT or NOW/TODAY that force a full recalculation, and replace them where a non-volatile formula would do.
Select unused rows/columns and clear their formatting — formatting applied to whole rows or columns bloats file size.

steps.t: Switch to manual calculation for a big edit
steps.d: Temporarily set calculation to Manual while making bulk changes to a large workbook, then recalculate once at the end.
